To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF) is nitric oxide (NO), (2) NO is produced by NO synthase (NOS) and (3) NO activates guanylyl cyclase to increase the concentration of cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP).

(i) the endothelium-dependent hyperpolarization of the rat renal artery is mediated by a novel mechanism, which involves a release of a diffusible factor that activates the smooth muscle large-conductance Ca2+-activated K+ (BK) channel; (ii) the endothelial cells are involved in this response; and (iii) the endothelial factor responsible for the activation of smooth muscle BK channel is a cytochrome P-450 metabolite of arachidonic acid

the endothelial-derived hyperpolarising factor (EDHF) is the most important vasodilator factor in the rat renal artery, and that EDHF-mediated vasodilator effects are dependent on gap junctions and the release of arachidonic acid.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the effect of endothelium-derived relaxing factors (nitric oxide, prostacyclin, and endothelium-derivedhyperpolarizing factor) on the contractile responses of the rat renal artery to noradrenaline and potassium.
the development of novel methods for the synthesis of biologically active compounds, including those with anticancer activity.
the role of endothelium-derived relaxing factors (EDRFs) in the vasodilatory response of the rat isolated renal artery to acetylcholine (ACh).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
gap junctions play a role in the EDHF-mediated vasodilation in the renal artery.
the role of the endothelium-derived factors in the regulation of renal blood flow is still not clear and that further studies are necessary to understand this issue.

the role of EETs and EDHF in mediating the endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF)-mediated relaxation in the rat aorta and renal artery are different, and that the role of gap junctions is more important in the renal artery than in the rat aortic rings.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the endothelium-derived nitric oxide and endothelium-dependent hyperpolarizing factors (EDHFs) mediate the vasodilatatory effects of bradykinin in rat renal artery and that the gap junctions are involved in EDHF-mediated vasodilatory response.

the role of the endothelium in the renal artery is to mediate vasodilatations by endothelium-derived relaxing factors, which are released from the endothelium by a variety of stimuli, including acetylcholine, histamine, substance P, bradykinin, adenosine and shear stress.
we are able to identify a novel mechanism by which the endothelium can control the contractility of the underlying smooth muscle.
The main takeaway from our work is that

gap junctions are important in endothelium-dependent hyperpolarizing-factor (EDHF) vasodilatations in the renal arteries, but that this effect is not mediated by the gap junction protein, connexin 37.
the endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF) is nitric oxide.
the role of endothelium-derived nitric oxide in mediating vasodilation is much more complex than previously appreciated.
